question: What conflicting claims do browser-automation communities make about stealth patches preventing bot detection, and which publicly reproducible observations support or contradict those claims?

claims.text: The `puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth` README makes a broad success claim, saying `puppeteer-extra with stealth passes all public bot tests` and that all `fpscanner`, `bot.sannysoft.com`, and `areyouheadless` tests were green in `v2.1.2`.

evidence_passages.text: `puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth` says `puppeteer-extra with stealth passes all public bot tests`, and the same README says all `fpscanner`, `bot.sannysoft.com`, and `areyouheadless` tests were green in `v2.1.2`.

claims.text: The same `puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth` README also qualifies that claim by saying there are still ways to detect headless Chromium and that it is `probably impossible to prevent all ways` to detect it.
acceptable_patterns: still ways to detect headless Chromium
probably impossible to prevent all ways

evidence_passages.text: the `puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth` README also says there are still ways to detect headless Chromium and that it is “probably impossible to prevent all ways” to detect it.

claims.text: The `selenium-stealth` project makes a similarly broad claim, saying it can `prevent almost all selenium detections` and that `selenium-stealth with stealth passes all public bot tests`.

evidence_passages.text: `selenium-stealth` says it can `prevent almost all selenium detections` and that `selenium-stealth with stealth passes all public bot tests`.

claims.text: The `undetected-chromedriver` repository makes an even broader claim, saying it does not trigger anti-bot services like Distill, Imperva, DataDome, and Botprotect.io, and that it `Passes ALL bot mitigation systems`.

evidence_passages.text: `undetected-chromedriver` describes itself as an optimized Selenium Chromedriver patch that does not trigger anti-bot services like Distill, Imperva, DataDome, and Botprotect.io, and its repository “About” text says `Passes ALL bot mitigation systems (like Distil / Imperva / Datadadome / CloudFlare IUAM)`.

claims.text: Public reproducible observations also show that modern detection discussions extend beyond classic stealth patches: Rebrowser says automation libraries use the CDP command `Runtime.Enable`, published `rebrowser-bot-detector` to verify such leaks, and acknowledges limitations in its proposed fixes.

evidence_passages.text: Automation libraries like Puppeteer and Playwright use the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) command `Runtime.Enable` to discover execution contexts needed for running JavaScript. This command triggers a `Runtime.consoleAPICalled` event that anti-bot systems can detect with minimal code, revealing browser automation activity.

Rebrowser published "rebrowser-bot-detector" alongside existing third-party detection pages. This tool enables developers to verify whether their automation setup leaks CDP signals to detection systems.

Acknowledged Limitations
- **Isolated worlds**: Cannot access main context variables; incompatible with web workers
- **Enable/Disable approach**: Brief vulnerability window exists where detection code could theoretically execute
- **Fragility**: Patches require maintenance as library source code evolves

rejected_claims.text: Stealth patches broadly prevent bot detection on modern defended sites.
rejected_claims.reason: Overly broad and contradicted by public issue reports in the supplied evidence, including `https://github.com/berstend/puppeteer-extra/issues/867`, `https://github.com/berstend/puppeteer-extra/issues/898`, and `https://github.com/ultrafunkamsterdam/undetected-chromedriver/issues/46`.

rejected_claims.text: Passing public bot-test pages proves a stealth patch prevents production bot detection generally.
rejected_claims.reason: Unsupported by the supplied evidence; the evidence only shows community claims about public tests and separate contradiction reports on real targets.

rejected_claims.text: `Runtime.Enable` detection still works everywhere in the same way.
rejected_claims.reason: Time-unstable and contradicted by the supplied Castle summary at `https://blog.castle.io/why-a-classic-cdp-bot-detection-signal-suddenly-stopped-working-and-nobody-noticed/`, which says a classic CDP detection implementation stopped working after May 2025 V8 changes.

rejected_claims.text: Stealth patches are always worse than vanilla automation.
rejected_claims.reason: Unsupported by the supplied evidence; no controlled head-to-head comparison in the provided passages establishes that universal claim.

rejected_claims.text: Public issue reports contradict broad stealth claims: a January 2024 `puppeteer-extra` issue says the README example itself was detected on `bot.sannysoft.com`, and the reporter also said `Cloudflare detects puppeteer too`.
rejected_claims.reason: Not supported by any supplied evidence passage. The Codex run opened zero URLs and its tool results carry no payloads; all 20 of its evidence_passages are identical copies of its own final_answer, truncated at 'playwright_stealth says: "Don't expec"' — i.e. before any contradiction bullet. The distinguishing specifics (issue #867, date 'January 10, 2024', and the quoted string 'Cloudflare detects puppeteer too') therefore rest solely on the drafting model's unretrieved assertion. The Claude run documents Cloudflare-failure issues at #811, #920 and #793, corroborating the theme but not this issue or quote. The pattern 'README example itself was detected on `?bot\.sannysoft\.com`?' is also overly narrow, requiring near-verbatim reproduction of one paraphrase's wording and clause order.

rejected_claims.text: Public issue reports also show version-sensitive failures: a June 2024 `puppeteer-extra` issue says `puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth` worked for Google Meet with Puppeteer `22.1.0` and Chrome-for-Testing `121.0.6167.85`, but with Puppeteer `22.2.0` and Chrome-for-Testing `122.0.6261.57` Google Meet detected automation and blocked access.
rejected_claims.reason: Same provenance defect: the issue #898 content falls past the truncation point of the Codex evidence passages, and the run retrieved no page text, so the highly specific date ('June 20, 2024') and version quadruple (Puppeteer 22.1.0 / Chrome-for-Testing 121.0.6167.85 vs Puppeteer 22.2.0 / 122.0.6261.57) are uncorroborated by anything in the supplied evidence. Nothing in the Claude run mentions Google Meet or these versions. Both acceptable_patterns are additionally too narrow for lexical grading, chaining four exact tokens in a fixed order that only one specific phrasing would satisfy.

rejected_claims.text: A public `undetected-chromedriver` issue also contradicts all-systems claims, reporting detection by Cloudflare `Under Attack Mode` and getting stuck on the `Checking your browser` page.
rejected_claims.reason: The undetected-chromedriver issue #46 report also lies beyond the truncation point of every Codex evidence passage, and that run retrieved no content from the URL it cites, so the date 'November 4, 2020' and the reported Cloudflare 'Under Attack Mode' / 'Checking your browser' outcome are unverifiable against the supplied evidence. The Claude run covers Cloudflare failures for puppeteer-extra but says nothing about undetected-chromedriver issue #46, so there is no cross-run support either. Rejected for lack of evidentiary grounding rather than pattern validity.
